extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers seeking an encyclopedic overview of Georg Cantor and his contributions to set theory
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style encyclopedic article summarizing Georg Cantor's life, mathematical work (especially the foundations of set theory), philosophical/religious context, and historical reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-to-one correspondence as criterion for same 'size' (cardinality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two sets are said to have the same 'size' if there exists a 1-to-1 correspondence between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cantor introduced the notion of 1‑to‑1 correspondence (bijection) and used it to formalize the concept of 'power' or equivalence of sets. Examples/explanations in the article: mapping between unit interval and n‑dimensional Euclidean space as a surprising instance where two sets of very different appearances have the same power. Emphasizes that bijections, not intuitive notions of size, are the mathematical standard for comparing sizes of infinite sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of countable (denumerable) and uncountable sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Countable (denumerable) sets are those that can be put into 1‑to‑1 correspondence with the natural numbers; nondenumerable (uncountable) sets are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cantor defined finite and infinite sets and subdivided infinite sets into denumerable and nondenumerable. He proved rationals are denumerable and reals are uncountable; the distinction is central to classifying infinite sets by cardinality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor's 1874 proof: real numbers are more numerous than the natural numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Cantor proved that the set of real numbers is 'more numerous' than the set of natural numbers, showing that infinite sets can have different sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes Cantor's two constructions: (1) enumerating algebraic numbers to show algebraic numbers are countable, and (2) given any sequence of real numbers, constructing nested intervals whose intersection contains a real not in the sequence — thus showing the reals cannot be listed. The constructions also yield explicit transcendental numbers (non-constructive vs constructive aspects are discussed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor's diagonal argument for uncountability
rubrics_metrics.description: The diagonal argument is a proof method that demonstrates the existence of uncountable sets (e.g., the reals) by constructing an element not in any purported list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites the 1891 diagonal argument and illustrates how the diagonal construction produces a sequence not appearing in any infinite list of sequences. It notes the diagonal argument's foundational role (e.g., in the Halting problem and Gödel's first incompleteness theorem) and distinguishes it from Cantor's earlier 1874 proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor's theorem (power set cardinality strictly larger)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any set A, the cardinality of the power set of A (the set of all subsets of A) is strictly larger than the cardinality of A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a central result establishing a hierarchy of infinite sets; Cantor used variants of the diagonal idea to prove this. The theorem underpins the richness of cardinal and ordinal arithmetic developed by Cantor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and use of 'power' or 'equivalence' of sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Cantor introduced the notion of 'power' (equivalence) of sets: two sets are equivalent (have the same power) if there is a 1‑to‑1 correspondence between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes Cantor took the term 'power' from Jakob Steiner and used it systematically to compare set sizes. This is the formal criterion used throughout his development of cardinalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuum hypothesis (CH) as a structural claim about cardinalities
rubrics_metrics.description: The continuum hypothesis asserts there is no set whose power is strictly greater than that of the naturals and strictly less than that of the reals (equivalently, the cardinality of the reals is exactly aleph-one).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cantor introduced CH and believed it true; the article summarizes later results (Gödel and Cohen) showing CH is independent of Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory with the axiom of choice (ZFC). The historical importance and Cantor's personal difficulties in proving CH are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well‑ordering principle / theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Cantor introduced the well‑ordering principle ('every set can be well‑ordered') and later attempted proofs (e.g., aleph theorem claiming every infinite set has cardinal an aleph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article records Cantor's attempts to prove the well‑ordering principle, his aleph theorem, and subsequent scrutiny and critique (Zermelo, von Neumann). It situates the well‑ordering claim as both philosophical and technical, and notes the role of the axiom of choice in Zermelo's later proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinal numbers as order types of well‑ordered sets and ordinal arithmetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinal numbers are defined as the order types of well‑ordered sets; Cantor defined addition and multiplication for ordinals and integrated ordinals into his theory of transfinite numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains how ordinals arise naturally (e.g., in derived sets S, S1, S2,... producing ω, ω+1, ...), how Cantor developed ordinal arithmetic, and how ordinals relate to the hierarchy of transfinite numbers. It also mentions extensions where order types generalize ordinals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties and role of the Cantor set and density examples
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cantor set is nowhere dense yet has the same cardinality as the real numbers; by contrast, the rationals are everywhere dense but countable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an example connecting topology to cardinality: nowhere denseness does not imply small cardinality. The article highlights Cantor's topological constructions and their role in illustrating cardinality phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bijections between Euclidean spaces of different dimensions (power of R^n equals R)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cantor proved that for any positive integer n, there exists a 1‑to‑1 correspondence between the points of the unit line segment and all the points in n‑dimensional space (R^n has the same power as R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes how counterintuitive this result is for geometric notions of dimension; it notes Cantor's own astonished reaction and that his explicit mappings are not continuous (important caveat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between sets and 'inconsistent multiplicities' to avoid paradoxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Cantor recognized two types of multiplicities: consistent multiplicities (sets) and inconsistent multiplicities (absolutely infinite collections); treating the latter as not sets avoids certain paradoxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains Cantor's approach to avoiding paradoxes (e.g., Burali‑Forti, Cantor's paradox) by recognizing big collections that cannot be treated as sets. It contrasts Cantor's strategy with Russell's (which led to paradoxes) and summarizes later formal set theories (Zermelo, von Neumann) that formalized restrictions on set formation to eliminate paradoxes.
